Summary

[
1
]        Mr. Darel, who is now ordinarily resident in
New York City, is approximately Cdn $700,000.00 in arrears of an Alberta child
and spousal support order. In this motion, he asks for “confirmation” of a request he has made to a New York
court for a downward modification of the Alberta order based on information
concerning his current financial circumstances. He also asks for an access
schedule to the children of the marriage.

[
2
]        In May 1994, Ms. Darel wrote to her husband
formally requesting, pursuant to the provisions of
s. 21.1
of the
Divorce
Act
, that he remove all barriers within his control that would prevent her
remarriage within her orthodox Jewish faith. In particular, she asked Mr. Darel
to complete whatever procedures were necessary to obtain a
Get
(marital
contractual release) from him. She received no response from Mr. Darel. No
Get

has been delivered to Ms. Darel.

[
3
]        Mr. Darel’s application for the “confirmation” of a request he
has made to a New York court is denied.

[
4
]        This court has no jurisdiction to entertain
Mr. Darel’s application.

[
5
]        In Canada, divorce comes within the
constitutional authority of the Federal Government; neither Alberta, nor any
province, can override federal legislation in matters relating to divorce.
(There is a political, but not always a constitutional analogy, between a

Canadian
province and an American state.) The federal legislator, Parliament,
has restricted the right to modify divorce judgments made by Canadian courts:
only Canadian courts can modify a Canadian divorce judgment. An American court
cannot vary a Canadian divorce judgment, even if that court is in a state which
is a reciprocating state for purposes of the
Reciprocal Enforcement of
Maintenance Orders Act

(REMO), which is provincial legislation.  The
Director of Maintenance Enforcement for Alberta invites my court to take
jurisdiction on this application; that office would like to cooperate with
American states in the matter of child support. However, this court is bound by
Parliament. Indeed, this very application demonstrates at least one potential
policy reason for Parliament’s limitation of confirmation proceedings under the
Divorce
Act
to Canadian courts: Parliament obviously intended to deal with the
thorny issue of religious divorce in a standardized way across Canada.

[
6
]        Moreover, in this case, no Judge or judicial
officer from the State of New York has approved Mr. Darel’s request for
variation of an existing court order. Strictly speaking, therefore, there is no
provisional order for this court to confirm. This is not a mere technical
breach of the
REMO
requirements.

[
7
]        The fact that Mr. Darel cannot move under
the confirmation provisions of the
Divorce Act
,
or the related
REMO

provisions, does not mean, of course, that Mr. Darel cannot ask an Alberta
court to modify its earlier decision. It only means that, in order to do so,
Mr. Darel will have to initiate proceedings in Alberta.

[
8
]        In this case, there is a strong likelihood
that the court would not exercise its jurisdiction to modify the existing order
at Mr. Darel’s request, even if it had such jurisdiction. Parliament has decided
that a person who fails to do what is within their power to do to facilitate a
religious divorce may not entitled to call upon the civil court for assistance
in the civil divorce proceedings. There may be no sufficient explanation from
Mr. Darel about his failure to grant his wife a
Get
.

1.         Background

[2]        The Divorce Judgment between the
parties, issued on March 28, 1995, ordered Mr. Darel to pay child support of
$2,500 per month for each of two children and $5,000 per month in spousal
support. The children of the marriage are now 15 and 12. The arrears of
interlocutory support at that time were $120,160.00. That judgment gave Mr.
Darel reasonable access to the children of the marriage, with access to be
exercised in the Province of Alberta.

[3]        Mr. Darel has not paid a penny of
support in 57 months. The arrears currently registered against him are,
approximately, Cdn $700,000.00.

[4]        Mr. Darel swears that when the
divorce judgment issued against him, by default, he had no money to contest the
divorce judgment or the amounts levied against him for corollary relief. He
says that he eventually left the United States, where he was living at the time
of the divorce judgment, to go to live with his family in Israel. He states
that he did not work for two years. He states that he returned to the State of
New York and found work with his brothers; he states that his salary at that
time was $1,500 per “pay period” without indication of the length of the
pay period. The material he files in support of his current application
indicates that his gross monthly earnings are approximately US $3,686.00.

[5]        On April 10, 1998, the Alberta
divorce judgment was registered under the Domestic Relations Law, Section 37A,
in the Family Court, New York County, New York. The document notifying Mr.
Darel of the registration of the
Canadian
order contained the following
information:

This order will be confirmed unless you file a
petition in this court within twenty (20) days from the date of mailing of this
notice setting forth reasons why this support order should be stayed, vacated
or re-opened.

When confirmed, this order will be payable to the
support collection unit in New York County and you are therefore directed to
send your payment forthwith to: Support Collection Unit - New York.

[6]        There is no indication on the
file that Mr. Darel filed a petition with the New York court within the
required 20 days.

[7]        Mr. Darel brings an “Initial Request” for a downward
modification of the existing support order; he grounds his request in the
Uniform Interstate Family Support Act (UIFSA) There is no material before the
court which explains the nature of the UIFSA or of the URESA which is
apparently an alternate form of interjurisdictional support enforcement.

[8]        The State of New York is a
reciprocating state within the meaning of the reciprocal enforcement of
maintenance legislation in Alberta.

[9]        Mr. Darel’s application does not contain any order
from any New York judicial officer. A person whose name is Suzanne Doherty and
who is described as the Initiating Contact Person and whose address is Central
Operations NYC - OCSE Interstate Case Unit, 2 Washington St. - 15
th

Floor - merely states:

We are filing a downward modification petition on
behalf of Mr. Darel based on his current income.

[10]      When Mr. Darel’s lawyer wrote
to the Clerk of this court to make inquiries about the state of the file, he
said:

On March 23,1999 we forwarded one original and three
copies of Petitioner’s Dror Darel, Uniform Support Petition, including
Child Support Enforcement Transmittal and General Testimony with attachments.

[
11
]      In other words, Mr. Darel himself
does not suggest that there is an order from a New York judicial officer that
grants him, albeit provisionally, the downward modification that he requests.

[
12
]      Mr. Darel swears that he retained a
lawyer for the purpose of trying to resolve the arrears and ongoing support
based on his current reality. He states that he had debts from his business
activities of US $2,600,000.00. He filed for bankruptcy; he was discharged from
bankruptcy on April 29, 1998. The discharge did not relieve Mr. Darel of sales
tax obligations of US $132,000 from his prior business.

[
13
]      Mr. Darel is not on public
assistance in the United States

[
14
]      Mr. Darel indicates that he is the
manager of Artrageous Gallery Inc., located in New York, N.Y., which is owned
by a relative, and that his estimated gross monthly earnings are US$3,686.00.
He states that his domestic partner’s gross monthly income is approximately
US$9,633.34. In rough translation into
Canadian
currency, the father’s gross monthly
income is approximately Cdn. $5,486 and his partner’s gross monthly income is Cdn.$14,400.

[
15
]      Coincidentally, I have previously
dealt with the Darel matter; I issued the support order in 1993. I recalled
that information had previously been put before the court concerning Ms. Darel’s request for a
religious divorce. On November 2, 1999, I asked her lawyer to remind me of the
information available concerning her request for a religious divorce. The
following is the information provided in answer to that request. In 1994, Ms.
Darel wrote to Rabbi Asher Vale at the Beth Israel Synagogue in Edmonton,
Alberta as follows:

I was married to my husband, Dror Darel, in an
orthodox wedding in Tel Aviv, Israel on March 20, 1983.

I wish to indicate my willingness to consent to
remove all barriers that are within my control and will prevent my spouse’s remarriage
with Judaism, by signifying herein my desire to accept a
Get
from him.

I confirm that this letter is the only step I need
to take in order to remove all barriers to my husband’s remarriage before commencing the
Get

procedure and that I now have done everything possible to remove such barriers.

[
16
]      On the same date, Ms. Darel wrote
to her husband as follows:

Pursuant to
Section 21.1
of the
Divorce Act of
Canada
,
1985, C.4
, and amendments thereto, I hereby make upon you a formal
request that you remove all barriers that are within your control and that
would prevent my remarriage within my faith.

For your information, in my case such removal would
entail your contacting my rabbi, Rabbi Asher Vale, at telephone number (403)
488-2840, immediately and completing whatever procedures are necessary in order
for me to obtain from you a
Get
(marital contractual release) so as to
permit a religious remarriage in my faith.

Pursuant to
Section 21.1
of the
Divorce Act of
Canada
, if you fail to honour this request, then I may take the appropriate
remedies pursuant to the same Act.

I would also inform you that you may attend before
any Orthodox Rabbi and appoint him unconditionally to act as your agent to
deliver to me a
Get
which you would execute. If you follow this
procedure, please have your Rabbi agent contact Rabbi Vale.

[
17
]      In an affidavit filed with this
court in August 1994, Mr. Darel swore:

13. I deny having taken steps to grant a religious
divorce to the Respondent. In fact, I phoned the Respondent’s Rabbi on a
number of occasions leaving messages for him to return my calls collect with
respect to this matter. He has never returned my calls.

[
18
]      It may be that the affidavit is
poorly worded and that Mr. Darel intended to swear that he denied having denied
Ms. Darel a religious divorce.

[
19
]      In April 1995, Ms. Darel wrote to
her husband’s then lawyer reminding him that Ms. Darel’s Rabbi had been instructed to complete
the “Jewish
divorce” on her end and that Mr. Darel should have his Rabbi contact her Rabbi
directly and provide him with the necessary paper work.

[
20
]      Ms. Darel has never received a
Get
.
Although she has a civil divorce judgment, she is unable to remarry within her
orthodox Jewish faith.

2.         Does the court have
jurisdiction to entertain a New York order for modification of an Alberta
decision?

[
21
]      Assuming, for the purpose of this
application, that this court had been provided with an order from a New York
court provisionally modifying the Alberta court’s spousal and child support order, would
this Alberta court have the jurisdiction to assess that provisional order and
confirm it?

[
22
]      The short answer to this question
is “No”. In answering
the question in that way, I adopt the  reasons given by Klebuc J. in his 1995
decision in
Cain
:

Counsel for the Attorney General agreed the
provisions of s. 8 of
The Reciprocal Enforcement of Maintenance Orders Act,
1983
do not apply because they deal with registered orders but argued that
s. 6 of
The Reciprocal Enforcement of Maintenance Orders Act, 1983

authorizes this Court to make confirmation orders once the Minister receives
documents from a reciprocating state pertaining to the confirmation of an order
purporting to vary a divorce support order. In my view the provisions of s. 6
do not apply because the province has no authority to expose a divorce order to
variation under provincial legislation in the first instance.
Section 20(3)
of
the
Divorce Act
contemplates the registration of divorce orders in
provincial courts and their enforcement
in a province
according to the
laws of that province. The phrase
enforced in a province
does not
contemplate the variation of divorce orders by provincial courts except as
provided for in
s. 18
of the
Divorce Act
, nor does s. 20(3) of the
Divorce
Act
authorize a province to register such orders in another jurisdiction
for enforcement in that jurisdiction.

[Emphasis in original]

[
23
]      I am not aware of any decision in
any province in Canada to the contrary.

[
24
]      There are, of course, many
decisions dealing with
REMO
legislation, including my own in the
Selander

and
Attrill
cases , which uphold the right of a
Canadian

court to apply REMO legislation to proceedings dealing with support orders
arising in divorce situations. However, none of these decisions deal with
Canadian divorce judgments that are purportedly modified by non-Canadian
courts. If the Darels had never married, or were not divorced, there may well
be jurisdiction for this court to act under the REMO legislation. If Mr. Darel
had moved to Saskatchewan instead of New York, there may well have been
jurisdiction for this court to act under the REMO legislation. If the Darels
had been living in the State of New York when the divorce judgment and support
orders were issued in that state, and Mr. Darel had re-established himself in
Alberta, there may well have been jurisdiction for this court to act under the
REMO legislation. However, those are not the facts of this case.

[
25
]      The Director of Maintenance
Enforcement invites me to take jurisdiction in this case, to do something
creative to take jurisdiction. The court is not able to ignore constitutionally
valid statutory limits on jurisdiction.

[
26
]      Nor would it be appropriate for a
court to undermine Parliament’s stated policy in this area. It may well be that
Parliament was concerned, for example to establish a national standard
concerning the approach to religious divorce and did not want
Canadian
citizens
who come within the protection of
s. 21.1
of the
Divorce Act
to be put
to the anxiety and expense of an application to vary an existing Canadian
divorce judgment where the person applying may be in breach of the policy
underlying s. 21.1 of the Act.

[
27
]      The fact that Mr. Darel cannot move
under the confirmation provisions of the
Divorce Act
,
or the related

REMO
provisions, does not mean, of course, that Mr. Darel cannot ask an Alberta
court to modify its earlier decision. It only means that, in order to do so,
Mr. Darel will have to initiate proceedings in Alberta. Should Mr. Darel
proceed in the ordinary way to bring himself within the jurisdiction of this
court to grant variations of existing decisions, Ms. Darel would be entitled to
the procedures available in this jurisdiction, including the right of
disclosure and the right to ask for security for costs.

[
28
]      I note, as well, that Mr. Darel
appears to have adequate financial means to bring his application for variation
in Alberta, under the normal process. This is not, therefore, a case in which
an Alberta court must address the social utility of reciprocal enforcement
legislation in situations of persons with limited financial means. Despite the
invitation of the Director, there is, on the facts of this case, no temptation
for the court to try to avoid the full impact of a clear constitutional limit
on jurisdiction.

3.         Is the material forwarded to
Alberta a
“
Provisional Order
”
within the meaning of the
Divorce Act
?

[
29
]      In the event, Mr. Darel did not
obtain an order from a New York court. Therefore, there is, strictly speaking,
nothing to confirm. All that has occurred is that a New York civil servant
passed along Mr. Darel’s application for a modification.

[
30
]      This is not an order of the type
accepted by our Court of Appeal in
Barbe
. It will be recalled
that, in that case, the only problem was that there was no transcript of the
evidence taken before the judicial officer. Our Court of Appeal held that there

[
31
]      Nor is this a case like

St.
Lawrence
where there was a concern that what had happened in New York
was merely a recommendation. Interestingly, however, for purposes of
comparison, that decision also arose out of variation proceedings commenced in
New York. The facts outlined in that case include the following:

On July 30
th
, 1993, the Family Court in
the State of New York made a recommendation in the form of a Judge’s Certificate,
that the respondents, Shelley and Brent Branchaud be directed to pay support
for the child Rickey D. Lamberton, born November 15
th
, 1978 in the
amount of $343.00 per month plus medical coverage.

[
32
]      Here, there is not even a
recommendation, much less a Judge’s Certificate. Indeed, it may be that the
difference between this application and the forms of application dealt with in
some of the case law is that the application in
St. Lawrence
was
brought under URESA whereas this application was brought under UIFSA.

[
33
]      In any event, however, these are
examples of a
Canadian
superior court rectifying what Cooke J. refers to in
Stephens

as “excessive concern over technical matters” by a lower Canadian court. However, in
this case, there is more than a technical matter at stake: there is no decision
from any judicial officer. Indeed, this case is clearly distinguishable from
Stephens

on the facts. In that case, there was an order from a Virginia judge. Cooke J.
noted these factors:

It must be appreciated that [the Virginia judge] had
before him the Divorce Decree and a Virginia State document entitled Uniform
Support Petition signed by the applicant on May 11, 1991. In that Petition, the
petitioner sought an increase in support for the child to $400 per month from
$300 per month. That Petition contained some information relating to the mother’s income and
expenses.

[
34
]      In this case, the New York
authorities sent to Alberta only an Initial Request on a Uniform Support
Petition. There is no New York equivalent of J. Wesley McClintock III, a
Virginia judge, who examined the material filed before him and issued a
provisional order.

[
35
]      In this case, therefore, apart
altogether from the issue of jurisdiction, there is no provisional order from
the State of New York which could be confirmed by the Alberta courts.

4.         What is the effect on this application
of Ms. Darel
’
s request for a
Get
?

[
36
]      The relationship between religious
and civil divorces is, of course, a difficult one. Because of the
constitutional guarantees of religious freedom contained in the
Canadian
Charter of Rights and Freedoms
, legislation that purported to interfere
with an individual’s freedom of religious conscience would be unlikely
to survive
Charter
scrutiny.

[
37
]      Parliament has, however, addressed
this issue. It has given the civil divorce courts power to consider the issue
of the barrier of an unresolved religious divorce if the person who refuses to
give a religious divorce finds himself or herself in the situation where he or
she calls on the civil courts to assist him or her in the civil divorce
proceedings.

[
38
]      The issue of Ms. Darel’s inability to
obtain a
Get
from Mr. Darel has not been fully explored in the
proceedings. However, the evidence is clear that Ms. Darel has made a formal
request for a
Get
, explicitly referring to the provisions of the
Divorce
Act
, that Mr. Darel has not provided any genuine religious or conscientious
grunds for his refusal to give instructions for a
Get
, and that Ms.
Darel still has not received a
Get
.

[
39
]      Assuming that those facts held up
under further examination, this might indeed be a situation in which this civil
court would think it appropriate not to consider Mr. Darel’s request for a
modification of the existing divorce order.

[
40
]      Where the court is of the view that
it would be inappropriate to lend its support to a litigant who has improperly
withheld a religious divorce, this would constitute a preliminary objection
even to the litigant bringing an application for modification of an existing
judgment.

5.         Conclusion

[
41
]      The court has no constitutional
jurisdiction to deal with Ms. Darel’s application. In any event, there is no
provisional order to confirm. Also, there is a strong suggestion that the
problems relating to the granting of a religious divorce would constitute a
preliminary hurdle to this particular application.

6.         Costs

[
42
]      Ms. Darel, who has been successful
in opposing this application, is entitled to her costs of the proceeding.
Because the issues in this application are somewhat out of the ordinary, Ms.
Darel is entitled to accelerated costs; I award her $750.00 costs for this
hearing.

DATED
at Edmonton, Alberta this 24th day of
October, 1999.

J.C.Q.B.A.

APPENDIX
A: STATUTORY FRAMEWORK

Sections 17.1

and
18
of the
Divorce Act

state:

17.1.
Variation order by affidavit, etc.
-
Where both former spouses are ordinarily resident in different provinces, a
court of competent jurisdiction may, in accordance with any applicable rules of
the court, make a variation order pursuant to subsection 17(1) on the basis of
the submissions of the former spouses, whether presented orally before the
court or by means of affidavits or any means of telecommunication, if both
former spouses consent thereto.

18.(1) In this section and section
19, “Attorney
General”, in respect of a province, means

(a)       for the Yukon Territory, the member of the
Council of the Yukon Territory designated by the Commissioner of the Yukon
Territory,

(b)       for the Northwest Territories, the member
of the Council of the Northwest Territories designated by the Commissioner of
the Northwest Territories, and

(b.1)    for Nunavut, the member of the Executive
Council of Nunavut designated by the Commissioner of Nunavut, and

(c)        for the other provinces, the Attorney
General of the province, and includes any person authorized in writing by the
member or Attorn General to act for the member or Attorney General in the
performance of a function under this section or section 19;

“Provisional order” means an order made pursuant to
subsection (2).

(2) Provisional order. Notwithstanding paragraph
5(1)(a) and subsection 17(1), where an application is made to a court in a
province for a variation order in respect of a support order and

(a)       the respondent in the application is ordinarily
resident in another province and has not accepted the jurisdiction of the
court, or both former spouses have not consented to the application of section
17.1 in respect of the matter, and

(b)       in the circumstances of the case, the
court is satisfied that the issues can be adequately determined by proceeding
under this section and section 19, the court shall make a variation order with
or without notice to and in the absence of the respondent but such order is
provisional only and has no legal effect until it is conformed in a proceeding
under section 19 and, where so confirmed, it has legal effect in accordance
with the terms of the order confirming it.

(3)
Transmission
- Where a court in a
province makes a provisional order, it shall send to the Attorney General for
the province

(a)       three copies of the provisional order
certified by a judge or officer of the court;

(b)       a certified or sworn document setting out
or summarizing the evidence given to the court; and

(c)        a statement giving any available
information respecting the identification, location, income and assets of the
respondent.

(4)
Idem.
On receipt of the documents
referred to in subsection (3), the Attorney General shall send the documents to
the Attorney General for the province in which the respondent is ordinarily
resident.

(5)
Further evidence
- Where, during a
proceeding under section 19, a court in a province remits the matter back for
further evidence to the court that made the provisional order, the court that
made the order shall, after giving notice to the applicant, receive further
evidence.

(6)
Transmission
. - Where evidence is
received under subsection (5), the court that received the evidence shall
forward to the court that remitted the matter back a certified or sworn
document setting out or summarizing the evidence, together with such
recommendations as the court that received the evidence considers appropriate.

Sections 2
,
3
,
4

and
5
of the
Reciprocal Enforcement of Maintenance Orders Act
state:

2.(d)  "confirmation order" means a
confirmation order made under this Act or under the corresponding enactment of
a reciprocating state;

(i)  "order" means an order or
determination of a court providing for the payment of money as maintenance by
the respondent named in the order for the benefit of the claimant or a
dependant of the claimant named in the order, and includes the maintenance
provisions of an affiliation order;

(j)  "provisional order" means

(i)  an order of a court in Alberta that has no
force or effect in Alberta until confirmed by a court in a reciprocating state,
or

(ii)  a similar order made in a reciprocating state
for confirmation in Alberta;

(n)  "provisional order" means

(i)  a final order made in a reciprocating state and
filed under this Act or under the former Act with a court in Alberta,

(ii)  a final order deemed under section 2(3) to be
a registered order, or

(iii)  a confirmation order that is filed under
section 5(8).

3(1)  On application by a claimant before or after
the commencement of this Act, a court may, without notice to and in the absence
of a respondent, make a provisional order against the respondent.

(2)  An order under subsection (1) may only include
the maintenance provisions the court could have included in a final order in a
proceeding of which the respondent had notice in Alberta but in which he failed
to appear.

(3)  If a provisional order is made, a proper
officer of the court in Alberta shall send to the Attorney General for
transmission to a reciprocating state

(a)  3 certified copies of the provisional order,

(b)  a certified copy of the evidence given in the
proceeding or a sworn document setting out or summarizing the evidence given in
the proceeding,

(c)  a copy of the enactments under which the
respondent is alleged to have an obligation to maintain the claimant, and

(d)  a statement giving available information
respecting identification, location, income and assets of the respondent.

5(1)  If the Attorney General receives from a
reciprocating state documents corresponding to those described in section 3(3)
with information that the respondent is in Alberta, the Attorney General shall
designate a court in Alberta for the purpose of proceedings under this section
and shall forward the documents to that court.

(2)  On receipt of the documents referred to in
subsection (1), the court shall, whether the provisional order was made before
or after the commencement of this Act, serve a summons on the respondent in the
same manner as it would in a proceeding under the Domestic Relations Act for
the same relief, and shall proceed, taking into consideration the sworn
document setting out or summarizing the evidence given in the proceeding in the
reciprocating state.

(4)  At the conclusion of a proceeding under this
section, the court may make a confirmation order in the amount it considers
appropriate or make an order refusing maintenance to any claimant.

(6)  The court, before making a confirmation order
in a reduced amount or before refusing maintenance, shall decide whether to
remit the matter back for further evidence to the court that made the
provisional order.

Section 21.1
of
the
Divorce Act

states:

21.1 (1) Definition of “spouse”. - In this section, “spouse” has the meaning
assigned by subsection 2(1) and includes a former spouse.

(2) Affidavit re removal of barriers to religious
marriage. - In any proceedings under this Act, a spouse (in this section
referred to as the “deponent”) may serve on the other spouse and file
with the court an affidavit indicating

(a) that the other spouse is the spouse of the
deponent;

(b) the date and place of the marriage,
and the-official character of the person who solemnized the marriage;

(c) the nature of any barriers to the
remarriage of the deponent within the deponent's religion the removal of which
is within the other spouse's control;

(d) where there are any barriers to the
remarriage of the other spouse within the other spouse's religion the removal
of which is within the deponent's control, that the deponent

(i) has removed those barriers, and the
date and circumstances of that removal, or

(ii) has signified a willingness to
remove those barriers, and the date and circumstances of that signification;

(e) that the deponent has, in writing,
requested the other spouse to remove all of the barriers to the remarriage of
the deponent within the deponent's religion the removal of which is within the
other spouse's control;

(f) the date of the request described in
paragraph (e); and

(g) that the other spouse, despite the
request described in para-graph (e), has failed to remove all of the barriers
referred to in that paragraph.

(3)  Powers of court where barriers not
removed.-Where a spouse who has been served with an affidavit under subsection
(2) does not

(a) within fifteen days after that
affidavit is filed with the court or within such longer period as the court
allows, serve on the deponent and file with the court an affidavit indicating
that all of the barriers referred to in paragraph (2)(e) have been removed, and

(b) satisfy the court, in any additional
manner that the court may require, that all of the barriers referred to in
paragraph (2)(e) have been removed, the court may, subject to any terms that
the court considers appropriate,

(c) dismiss any application filed by that
spouse under this Act, and

(d) strike out any other pleadings and
affidavits filed by that spouse under this Act.

(4) Special case.-Without limiting the generality of
the court's discretion under subsection (3), the court may refuse to exercise
its powers under paragraphs (3)(c) and (d) where a spouse who has been served
with an affidavit under subsection (2)

(a) within fifteen days after that affidavit is
filed with the court or within such longer period as the court allows, serves
on the deponent and files with the court an affidavit indicating genuine
grounds of a religious or conscientious nature for refusing to remove the
barriers referred to in paragraph (2)(e); and

(b) satisfies the court, in any additional manner
that the court may require, that the spouse has genuine grounds of a religious
or conscientious nature for refusing to remove the barriers referred to in
paragraph (2)(e).

(5)  Affidavits.-For the purposes of this section,
an affidavit filed with the court by a spouse must, in order to be valid,
indicate the date on which it was served on the other spouse.

(6)  Where section does not apply. -This section
does not apply where the power to remove the barrier to religious remarriage
lies with a religious body or official.

I delivered judgment in the
instant case under date of November 5, 1993. With the consent and participation
of the petitioner, I agreed to hear counsel for the Attorney-General for
Saskatchewan regarding the applicability of
The
Reciprocal Enforcement of
Maintenance Orders Act, 1983, S.S. 1983, c.
R-4.1, to the variation and
confirmation of support orders made under the
Divorce Act
, R.S.C. 1985,
c.3 (2nd Supp.). Despite the persuasive arguments raised by the Attorney
General, I am, with great reluctance, unable to change the opinion expressed in
the judgment of November 5, 1993, namely that neither the
Divorce Act

nor any other legislation enacted by the Parliament of Canada authorizes or
tolerates the variation of divorce orders pursuant to
The
Reciprocal
Enforcement of Maintenance Orders Act
or similar legislation of
jurisdictions outside Canada, including
The Magistrates' Court Act
, 1980
[U.K.], and
The Maintenance Orders (Reciprocal Enforcement) Act
, 1972
[U.K.].

Counsel for the Attorney
General agreed the provisions of s. 8
of The' Reciprocal Enforcement of
Maintenance
Orders Act, 1983 do not apply because they deal with registered
orders but argued that s. 6 of
The Reciprocal Enforcement of Maintenance
Orders Act, 1983
authorizes this Court to make confirmation orders once the
Minister receives documents from a reciprocating state pertaining to the
confirmation of an order purporting to vary a divorce support order. In my view
the provisions of s. 6 do not apply because the province has no authority to
expose a divorce order to variation under provincial legislation in the first.
instance.
Section 20(3)
of the
Divorce Act

contemplates the registration
of divorce orders in provincial courts and their enforcement
in a province

according to the laws of that province. The phrase
enforced in a province
does
not contemp late the variation of divorce orders by provincial courts except as
provided for in
s. 18
of the
Divorce
Act, nor does s. 20(3) of the
Divorce
Act
authorize a province to register such orders in another jurisdiction
for enforcement in that jurisdiction. Accordingly, when the maintenance
enforcement officer of one province forwards a divorce support order to the
maintenance enforcement officer of another province, he or she is not
subjecting such order to the provisions of
The Reciprocal Enforcement of
Maintenance Orders Act,
1983, but merely facilitating the process
prescribed by ss. 18 and 20(3) of the
Divorce Act.

In my opinion, reciprocating
provinces may not use
The Reciprocal Enforcement of Maintenance Orders
Act,
1983 to vary or rescind divorce support orders in light of the procedures
contemplated provided for in the
Divorce Act
,
Without conceding the
point, counsel for the Attorney General suggested that
The Reciprocal
Enforcement of Maintenance Orders Act, 1983
nonetheless applied in the instant
case because the
Divorce Act
is silent regarding the registration of
divorce support orders in courts outside Canada and therefore the operational
conflict test in
Multiple Access Ltd. v. McCutcheon et al.,
[1982] 2
S.C.R. 138 D.L.R. (3d) 1
, can be met. I do not agree. The
Reciprocal
Enforcement of Maintenance Orders Act
, 1983 deals with more than
enforcement -- it provide's a regime whereby reciprocating jurisdictions may
provisionally vary each others judgments and orders. Canada is not a party
thereto, and therefore, cannot be viewed as a non-reciprocating jurisdiction.
Accordingly, to the extent that
The Reciprocal Enforcement of Maintenance
Orders Act,
1983 jeopardizes the integrity of divorce orders without the
express approval of Canada, it conflicts with the jurisdiction of the federal
government and cannot be applied: Gould v. Gould,
1980 CanLII 2123 (SK CA)
, [1980] 6 W.W.R. 506, 114
D.L.R. (3d) 646, 4 Sask. R. 129. If Parliament and the Legislature wish to
subject divorce support orders to variation in the manner contemplated by
The
Reciprocal Enforcement of Maintenance Orders Act,
1983, the
Divorce Act

must be amended to provide for the same.

Counsel cited the decisions
in
Larson v. Larson
(1992),
1992 CanLII 7869 (SK QB)
,
106
Sask. R. 257;
Barton v. Barton,
(1985)
1985 CanLII 2554 (SK QB)
,
44
Sask.
R.
272
; Hudson v. Santa Clara County, California
(1983),
1983 CanLII 2558 (SK CA)
, 32 R.F.L. (2nd)
367. These decisions deal solely with orders made under the legislation of
reciprocating states or provinces and therefore are not applicable in the
instant case.
